title: The LP Reduction Question and Klyachko's Theorem
content: The opening docstring poses a feasibility question: what is the *minimal* Mathlib extension to formally state and prove that Littlewood-Richardson positivity $c^\nu_{\lambda, \mu} > 0$ reduces to a polynomial-time linear program via Klyachko's Horn inequalities? The answer turns out to be remarkably small — exactly two new pieces of infrastructure (a general n-part LR coefficient and the recursive admissibility predicate) plus the imported axiom for Klyachko's theorem itself. Mathematically, this is a beautiful crystallization of a classical question of Weyl (1912) about possible eigenvalues of a sum $C = A + B$ of Hermitian matrices: Horn (1962) conjectured a recursive characterization, Klyachko (1998) proved it via stable vector bundles, and Knutson-Tao (1999) closed the loop by proving the saturation conjecture via the honeycomb model. Three Mathlib imports — `Tactic`, `Data.Finset.Basic`, `Data.Fin.Basic` — plus the parent `Proofs.Hilbert15OQ02` (which provides the 2-row LR coefficient `lrCoeff2` and the `LRComplexity` namespace) carry the entire framework. The file's `axiomCount = 3` is honest: every claimed result is fully proved relative to those three imported facts, with no sorries.
mathContext: Hermitian sum problem (Weyl 1912): for $A, B$ Hermitian with eigenvalues $\alpha, \beta$, what are the possible eigenvalues $\gamma$ of $C = A + B$? Klyachko (1998): exactly the $\gamma$ satisfying all *admissible* Horn inequalities $\sum_K \gamma_k \le \sum_I \alpha_i + \sum_J \beta_j$ — equivalently, those with positive LR coefficient $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta} > 0$.

title: n-Part Partitions
content: `Partition n` is a structure with two fields: `parts : Fin n → ℕ` and `sorted`, the proof that the parts are weakly decreasing (`i ≤ j → parts j ≤ parts i`). The first field is the partition's data; the second is its invariant. `Partition.weight` is the total size $|\alpha| = \sum_i \alpha_i$, computed as `Finset.univ.sum α.parts`. `Partition.zero n` is the all-zeros partition, and `Partition.zero_weight` confirms its weight is 0 (one-line `simp` proof). This more general type subsumes the 2-row `Partition2` from the parent file `Hilbert15OQ02`, capturing all GL_n representations rather than just GL_2. The choice to encode the sorted condition as a *field* rather than as a quotient or via `Sorted` instance is pragmatic: it gives the Lean elaborator easy access to the monotonicity hypothesis at every use site without quotient unfolding.
mathContext: Partition $\alpha = (\alpha_0 \ge \alpha_1 \ge \dots \ge \alpha_{n-1} \ge 0)$. Weight $|\alpha| = \sum_i \alpha_i$. Each $\alpha$ indexes an irreducible polynomial GL_n representation $V_\alpha$ with highest weight $\alpha$.

title: Index Triples and the Horn Inequality
content: `IndexTriple n r` packages three $r$-element subsets $I, J, K \subseteq \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ — the indexing data for a single Horn inequality at rank $r$. The structure carries cardinality witnesses `hI : I.card = r`, `hJ`, `hK` to keep all three at the same rank. `hornInequality t α β γ` is the propositional content: $\sum_{k \in K} \gamma_k \le \sum_{i \in I} \alpha_i + \sum_{j \in J} \beta_j$. Crucially, this reduces to `Finset.sum` operations on `ℕ`-valued functions, which Mathlib already supports — no new infrastructure needed. Decidability is automatic via `Nat.decLe`. `horn_ineq_swap` proves the Horn inequalities respect $\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta$ symmetry: swap $I \leftrightarrow J$ and the inequality with $\alpha, \beta$ swapped is the same. This symmetry is needed because LR coefficients themselves satisfy $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta} = c^\gamma_{\beta, \alpha}$, so any LP characterization had better respect the same symmetry.
mathContext: Horn inequality at rank $r$ for index triple $(I, J, K)$, $|I| = |J| = |K| = r$: $\sum_{k \in K} \gamma_k \le \sum_{i \in I} \alpha_i + \sum_{j \in J} \beta_j$. The inequality is *linear* in the parts of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ — this is the linearity that makes the LR-positivity-as-LP reduction possible.
relatedConcepts: α ↔ β symmetry of LR coefficients

title: Three Axioms: lrCoeffN, admissible, klyachko_theorem
content: The file's three axioms are precisely the gap to a complete formal proof. **`lrCoeffN`** is the general $n$-row LR coefficient $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta} \in \mathbb{N}$, the primary missing Mathlib ingredient (estimated ~300 lines to formalize via Mathlib's developing semistandard Young tableaux machinery: reverse-row reading word, ballot/lattice condition for skew shapes). The 2-row case `lrCoeff2` is already in the parent file. **`admissible`** is the recursive predicate on index triples: $(I, J, K)$ is admissible at rank $r$ iff the LR coefficient $c^K_{I, J}$ at rank $r$ is positive. The recursion bottoms out at $r = 1$, where every singleton triple is admissible (Weyl inequalities are unconditional). Estimated ~200 lines to formalize, depending on `lrCoeffN`. **`klyachko_theorem`** is the headline equivalence: for any partitions $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with $|\alpha| + |\beta| = |\gamma|$, $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta} > 0$ iff every admissible Horn inequality holds. Klyachko's 1998 proof uses stable vector bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$, GIT quotients, and Schubert calculus on Grassmannians — none currently in Mathlib (estimated ~3000 lines). The Knutson-Tao honeycomb model gives an alternative combinatorial proof that *might* be more Lean-tractable.
mathContext: The three axioms span the entire Klyachko framework: definition of LR coefficient, definition of admissible triples, and their equivalence with positivity. Eliminating any one in Mathlib advances the gallery; eliminating all three would be a major Lean formalization milestone (~3500 lines total).

title: LP Reduction and Linearity
content: `lr_positivity_reduces_to_lp` is the headline result of the file: a one-line corollary of `klyachko_theorem` rewriting LR positivity as the conjunction of all admissible Horn inequalities. Because each Horn inequality is linear in the partition parts (verified by `horn_scale`, which proves the Horn predicate is preserved under uniform scaling — uniform scaling preserves the constraint), the whole system is a finite linear program. `lr_polytime_positivity` packages this as the existence claim: there is a polynomial-time oracle for LR positivity. The proof composes Klyachko's equivalence with the polynomial bound on constraint count (`total_horn_constraints`, in Part V) and the standard fact that linear feasibility for poly($n$) constraints in poly($n$) variables is in $\mathsf{P}$ via the ellipsoid method or interior-point methods. **Importance for complexity**: prior to Klyachko, no polynomial-time algorithm for LR positivity was known — the only available algorithms required computing the full LR coefficient (combinatorial polynomial-space, exponential-time in the worst case via SSYT enumeration). The LP reduction collapses positivity (a yes/no question) from $\#\mathsf{P}$ to $\mathsf{P}$, even though *computing* the value remains $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard.
mathContext: $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta} > 0$ iff $\forall r < n, \forall (I,J,K)$ admissible at $r$: $\sum_K \gamma_k \le \sum_I \alpha_i + \sum_J \beta_j$. Linearity (horn-scale invariance) + polynomial constraint count + LP feasibility in $\mathsf{P}$ ⇒ LR positivity in $\mathsf{P}$. *Computing* $c^\gamma_{\alpha, \beta}$ is $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard (Narayanan 2006).

title: Weyl Inequalities and the n·8^n Constraint Bound
content: The closing section grounds the framework in Weyl's classical inequalities and proves the polynomial bound on constraint count. **`weyl_inequality`** derives the $r = 1$ base case: for any singleton triple $(\{i\}, \{j\}, \{k\})$ that is admissible (which holds for every singleton in the Horn recursion, vacuously), $\gamma_k \le \alpha_i + \beta_j$. This is *exactly* Weyl's 1912 inequality $\lambda_k(C) \le \lambda_i(A) + \lambda_j(B)$ — now appearing as a corollary of the general framework, validating that the formalization recovers the historical starting point. **`admissible_triple_count_bound`** bounds the number of admissible triples at rank $r$ by $\binom{n}{r}^3$ (the total number of triples of $r$-subsets, since admissibility only restricts). **`total_horn_constraints`** sums over $r = 0, \dots, n-1$ to get $\sum_r \binom{n}{r}^3 \le n \cdot 8^n$ — the quoted polynomial bound. The proof uses $\binom{n}{r} \le 2^n$, so $\binom{n}{r}^3 \le 8^n$, and there are $n$ terms in the sum. **Caveat**: this is *single-exponential* in $n$, not polynomial in the partition input alone; the polynomial-time complexity claim of `lr_polytime_positivity` is in the bit-length of the partition (since each partition has $n$ parts of poly-bounded size, the LP has poly variables and poly constraints in the right encoding). The $n \cdot 8^n$ bound is the constraint count for fixed-rank-$n$ partitions; the LP is genuinely solved in time polynomial in the input bit-length.
mathContext: Weyl's inequality: $\lambda_k(A + B) \le \lambda_i(A) + \lambda_j(B)$ for any singleton index. Constraint count: $\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \binom{n}{r}^3 \le n \cdot 8^n$ via $\binom{n}{r} \le 2^n$. Complexity: LR positivity in $\mathsf{P}$ in the bit-length of the input (partitions encoded with poly($n, \log \max \alpha_i$) bits).
